newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: RUGBY UNION-BOARD TIGHTEN ELIGIBILITY RULES.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-BOARD TIGHTEN ELIGIBILITY RULES.

text.p: Rugby union internationals will in future only be allowed to play for one country at the highest level after the sport's governing body tighted up the rules on Friday.

The International Rugby Football Board's (IRFB) 21-man council voted at the end of its five-day annual meeting to change its regulations on the eligibility of players for selection to senior national teams.

In a statement, the IRFB said the new ruling takes effect immediately and ensures that once a player has accepted an invitation to play for their national team, or the next level of senior team, they will never be able to represent another country.

Board chairman Vernon Pugh said: "This issue was raised by Carlos Tozzi of Argentina and reflects his union's concerns about the possible loss of leading players to other countries and the strong belief that representing one's country should be a choice for life.

"We realise this decision has the potential to cause hardship to players from any nation now in the process of requalifying for a second country by standing down from international rugby for 36 months, as was their right under the previous regulation."
Pugh said some players may have opted to play for a country in the knowledge and on the basis that it would be possible to play for another country after a three year stand-down period.

"We will be drafting the new regulation in such a way that any capped players who are now qualifying for another country, and have been living in a new country for a significant period of time, will still be able to complete the process. Any other approach would have the potential for being unfair," Pugh said.

Commenting on the hopes of Francois Pienaar, now with English club Saracens, winning an English cap, Pugh said: "As long as the former South African captain has been resident in England for a full three years, and does not play for any other country in the meantime, then he will be able to play for England."

The IRFB said the scrummage law had been altered to ensure the player whose feet are the "hindmost" -- normally the number eight -- must bind with at least one arm onto one of his lock forward team mates.

The Board also said in recognising the increased pace of the game of rugby union that had come with revised laws and the advent of full-time professionalism, it had doubled the permitted maximum duration of the halftime interval to 10 minutes.
